newsitem.title: MONGOLIA: FEATURE-Mongolia wants own plant to process copper.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Mongolia wants own plant to process copper.

text.p: Mongolia wants to take another step away from more than seven decades of dependence on its big neighbour, Russia. It wants to process its own copper.
Copper concentrate is the biggest single export from this land-locked nation that is three times the size of France but has just 2.3 million people.

But with doubt hanging over the capacity of the copper industry to maintain profits, the Ministry of Agriculture and Industry wants to build a plant to process at least half of Mongolia's concentrate at home by the end of the century.

Domestic production is essential to ensure a profit and to cut costs as the percentage of pure copper in concentrate mined in Mongolia has fallen to 25-30 percent from a previous 35 percent, officials said.

"We have an immediate need to get a plant where 50 to 60 percent of concentrate we produce can be processed into copper," T. Battseren, deputy director of the ministry's mining department, said in an interview.
He said he wanted to see a plant in operation by 2000.
ALL CONCENTRATE NOW PROCESSED IN RUSSIA
Currently, all copper concentrate is sent to Russian refineries from the huge Erdenet mine, Mongolia's only mine and a joint venture with Russia.

In 1996, Mongolia exported 486,100 tonnes of copper concentrate from the mine, up from 446,200 tonnes in 1995. That included some concentrate taken from stockpiles both years as its total production in 1996 was just 351,500 tonnes, up from 346,400 tonnes the previous year.
The amount of concentrate mined was expected to increase while annual production of pure copper would remain steady at about 121,000 tonnes, Battseren said.
The Erdenet mine in northern Mongolia is an open cast mine where the percentage of copper declines as mining goes deeper.
Mongolia has found more copper in its Central Gobi province, but the government has no plans to exploit the deposit, about one-fifth the size of Erdenet, Battseren said.
Erdenet holds reserves for another 50 to 60 years at current production levels, he said.

The mine needs foreign investment and technology to develop large-scale domestic processing, a proposal under discussion with several foreign companies including Outokumpu of Finland, he said, but declined to identify the other firms.
"Outokumpu seems to be the closest partner and the most realistic," Battseren said.
The biggest problems are financing for a plant and updating ageing equipment at the mine, he said.
"To prevent production falling, we need investment of $240 million," Battseren said.
Mongolia is also discussing the investment with its Russian mining partners, but has yet to reach a final decision.
PROFITS DESPITE HIGH COSTS
Currently, production costs at the mine account for 60 percent of revenue while taxes, customs duties and other costs take up some of the remaining 40 percent, he said.
"However, last year actual profit was more than 10 billion tugriks ($13.9 million)," Battseren said.
Profit is divided between the joint venture mining partners on the basis of equity, with 51 percent going to Mongolia and 49 percent to Russia.
Revenues could soar if Mongolia could refine at least some of the copper domestically, Battseren said.
A U.S.-Mongolia joint venture processing plant, Erdmin, is expected to start production at the Erdenet mine in the first quarter of this year, with output at 3,000-3,600 tonnes a year.
However, operations are limited by infrastructure problems such as power shortages, although once-regular black-outs had declined in the past six months.
"There is little hope that the problems would be fully solved," Battseren said.
Mongolia has initial plans to build a hydro-power plant on the Egiin River in northern Mongolia to support its Central Electricity System, which now imports electricity for peak demand from Russia.
Battseren said road connections would improve soon with a new highway connecting Erdenet to the northern city of Darkhan to be completed in a few years.
The mine currently transports concentrate by rail.
In addition, the mine is awaiting overdue payments for its concentrate from companies in Russia and Kazakhstan. "It is a question of dozens of millions (of dollars)," Battseren said.
Repayment would do little more than enable Erdenet to pay off what it owes to other Mongolian companies, he said.
However, Battseren remains optimistic about the planned processing plant. "Nothing is impossible," he said.
